subtype: Approach: trying to become friends with the bully [Thinking]
passage: Wednesday night. Irfan called my glasses "bottle bottoms" again today. I nearly cried, but then I noticed something: nobody sits with Irfan at lunch, ever. Maybe that's why. Maybe lonely people get mean. First thing in the morning I told Ms Dsouza, because Amma says grown-ups must know. She wrote it down. Then at lunch I said, "Nice drawing," about the dinosaur on Irfan's folder. Irfan blinked and said "thanks", and said nothing mean all lunch! But at the bus stop it started again. So a kind word isn't magic. Telling Ms Dsouza matters more. Tomorrow I'll tell her about the bus too. Trisha

qa.q: What did Trisha say to Irfan at lunch?
qa.a: Trisha said "Nice drawing" about the dinosaur on Irfan's folder.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when Irfan mocked the glasses, and what changed the thought?
qa.a: Trisha felt hurt and nearly cried, but noticing that nobody sits with Irfan made Trisha wonder whether loneliness was behind the teasing.

qa.q: What should Trisha do besides trying kind words, and why?
qa.a: Keep telling Ms Dsouza, including about the bus, since the kind word only worked sometimes and an adult can deal with the teasing itself.

qa.q: What might lunch be like for Irfan?
qa.a: Lonely, because nobody sits with Irfan, so a kind comment about the folder may have been a rare friendly moment, which fits the surprised blink and the "thanks".

grounding: Trisha wonders if the bully is lonely, tells a teacher, and also tries a kind word, seeing it is not a substitute for adult help.
